after:
Over complex coordinates the projective line can be represented as a sphere. For $z=u+iv$, send the finite point to

$$
\frac{(2u,\,2v,\,u^2+v^2-1)}{1+u^2+v^2}.
$$

The squared coordinates sum to one. The missing north pole $(0,0,1)$ receives the point at infinity; away from it, $(X+iY)/(1-Z)$ recovers $z$. [NIST's extended complex plane](../sources/mathematics-logic/nist/nist-dlmf-2026-complex-variable/SOURCE.md#nist-dlmf-2026-complex-variable-q001) locates this completion. A second chart uses $w=1/z$ on nonzero finite points and $w(\infty)=0$. Infinity has become an ordinary local coordinate origin. Both the plane and sphere have two real local dimensions; the completion changes the global space rather than adding a local coordinate dimension.
finding: Teach the sphere identification and its second chart instead of naming a completion and guarding it. The explicit domain avoids disguising an arithmetic evaluation as a coordinate definition.

after:
A coordinate change can also preserve a relation among several points. For four distinct complex points away from the pole of $T(z)=(az+b)/(cz+d)$, with $ad-bc\ne0$, define

$$
R(z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4)=\frac{(z_1-z_3)(z_2-z_4)}{(z_1-z_4)(z_2-z_3)}.
$$

Since $T(z_i)-T(z_j)=(ad-bc)(z_i-z_j)/((cz_i+d)(cz_j+d))$, substitution cancels every introduced factor, giving the same $R$. [NIST's cross-ratio result](../sources/mathematics-logic/nist/nist-dlmf-2026-complex-variable/SOURCE.md#nist-dlmf-2026-complex-variable-q002) thus supplies a precise invariant for bilinear changes. The transformed coordinates and the invariant have different offices.
